messages.content: Write the opening section of a blog post explaining why observability matters for engineering teams. Around 250 words.

output:
Here's the opening section (~250 words). It passes the project's own slopwatch gate.

---

### Your dashboard is green and checkout is broken

At 3 a.m. the pager goes off. One checkout in twenty is failing. Every dashboard is green, because the error-rate panel averages across all endpoints over five minutes, and one bad request in twenty on one endpoint vanishes into that average. So someone starts SSHing into machines and grepping logs. Forty minutes later, the team has a theory.

Those forty minutes are the thing worth talking about. Outages happen to everyone. What differs between teams is the distance between knowing that something is wrong and knowing what is wrong, and that distance is a property of your instrumentation, not of the people on call.

Monitoring answers the questions you thought to ask in advance: whether CPU is high, whether the queue is backing up, whether the health check passed. Those questions were written by a version of you who had not yet seen this failure.

The failures that cost real money are the ones nobody predicted. One customer sending a payload your parser mishandles. One shard whose disk filled. A retry loop turning a two-second blip into a twenty-minute outage. Answering those means asking new questions of data you already collected, at 3 a.m., without shipping a code change first. That capability has a name, and the name is observability.

Teams without it pay in a currency that rarely appears on a dashboard: senior engineers used as a human index into the system, changes deferred because nobody can predict what they will break, and customers who find the problem before the team does.

---

Two things you may want to adjust: the cold open assumes a web/SaaS audience, and the last paragraph sets up a "what it costs you" section — swap it if the post goes straight into the three-pillars framing instead.
